profile.name: Cajun Jig
profile.tagline: A simple, bouncy Cajun partner dance from Louisiana built on a single stepping pattern.
profile.insight: Danced as if a nail pierces one heel, the Cajun Jig transforms a slight, limping hop into an endlessly variable partner dance.
profile.profile: The Cajun jig, also known as the Cajun one-step, is among the simplest of Cajun dance forms and features only one basic step. Popularized in Louisiana during the late 1980s and early 1990s, it remains a vibrant mainstay for dancers today. Danced to fast or slow music in 2/4 or 4/4 timing, the dance allows for infinite variations through handhold changes and turns. It shares a vague similarity to the Merengue and is frequently alternated with other dance styles within a single song.
profile.profile_long:
The Cajun jig or Cajun one-step stands as one of the simplest and most enduring forms of Cajun dance. Originating and flourishing as a popular fixture in Louisiana during the late 1980s and early 1990s, it continues to be practiced actively by regular dancers, particularly in urban and non-traditional settings, as well as by Zydeco dancers. Its hallmark is a single fundamental step sequence that can be seamlessly alternated with other dance styles during the course of a single song.

The music accompanying the Cajun jig is played under 2/4 or 4/4 timing, aligning with the two-step rather than one-step blues time or the 3/4 timing associated with the waltz. It can be performed at either fast or slow tempos. Traditional audio documentation, such as performances by Marc Savoy and Michael Doucet, highlights its roots in traditional Cajun style.

Physically, the dance begins by marching with the left foot in place, to the side, forward, and back to the starting point. Dancers then adopt a distinctive posture as if a nail were embedded in one heel, causing that foot to touch down only on the toes with a slight limp that produces a bouncing visual effect. This injured heel can be varied and alternated. On the count of "one," the toes of the active foot touch down while the body straightens; on "two," the dancer drops onto the flat foot.

Despite having only a single basic step, the dance offers infinite movement options through variations in handholds and turns. Partners can use uncrossed handholds—where the right hand of one meets the left hand of the other and vice versa—or crossed handholds, such as joined right hands over left or left over right. This adaptability makes it a dynamic presence in both traditional and contemporary social dance environments.

sections.origins_and_history: The Cajun jig was especially popular in Louisiana in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and it remains a mainstay of dancers today in urban, non-traditional, and regular social settings.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers begin marching with the left foot in place, to the side, forward, and back. They then adopt a limping, bouncing motion as if a nail were in one heel, touching down on the toes on 'one' while straightening the body, and falling onto the flat foot on 'two'.
sections.music_and_instruments: Played to fast or slow Cajun music under 2/4 or 4/4 timing, associated with the two-step rather than waltz or blues timing.
sections.costume_and_setting: Danced in urban and non-traditional settings by regular dancers and Zydeco enthusiasts.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Mainstay of regular dancers, often alternated with other styles during a single song.

basic_steps: Marching beginning with the left foot in place, to the side, forward, and back.
Stepping with a slight limp as if a nail is in one heel, touching only on the toes to create a bouncing image.
On count one, touch the toes of the active foot and straighten the body.
On count two, drop onto the flat foot.
teaching.level_notes: Among the simplest of Cajun dance forms, highly beginner-friendly.

music_profile.sound_description: Cajun music played under 2/4 or 4/4 timing, associated with the two-step, performed at fast or slow tempos.

movement_profile.posture: Body straightens on the count of one when the toe touches down.
movement_profile.footwork: Marching beginning with left, in place, to the side, forward, and back, followed by a toe-touch and flat-foot drop simulating a nail in the heel.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Handholds can be uncrossed or crossed (joined right hands over left, or left over right) combined with turns.
movement_profile.partnering: Partner dance utilizing uncrossed or crossed handholds and various turns.

signature_moves.name: Nail-in-heel step
signature_moves.description: Stepping with a toe touch and slight limp as if a nail is in the heel, creating a bouncing image.

episode_brief.logline: Explore the simplest Cajun dance form, where a single limping step opens up infinite partner variations.
beats: Introduction to the Cajun jig's popularity in Louisiana during the late 1980s and 1990s.
Breaking down the basic marching step and the nail-in-the-heel bouncing image.
Listening to traditional Cajun music in 2/4 and 4/4 timing.
Experimenting with uncrossed and crossed handholds.
Combining turns and alternating styles within a single song.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master the basic marching and nail-in-heel weight shift.
drills: Marching left in place, to the side, forward, and back.
Practicing the toe touch on count one and flat foot drop on count two.

seniors.seated_version: Seated marching in place starting with the left foot, tapping toes on count one and placing feet flat on count two.
seniors.standing_version: Standing with support, practicing the basic weight shift from toes to flat foot without vigorous bouncing.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Reduced tempo and range of motion.
seniors.counts: Count one for toe touch, count two for flat foot drop.

children.game_version: A mirroring game where children march left and practice stepping with a light toe touch as if avoiding a sticky spot on their shoe.
children.counts: 1, 2 counting for toe touch and flat foot drop.
